1.pericope_label: Plead my cause, O Lord, with them that strive with me: fight against them that fight against me. Take hold of shield and buckler, and stand up for mine help

schools.summary: Delitzsch pairs the psalm with the one before, assigns it to the Saul persecution, and rejects the Jeremiah conjecture; Ellicott presses the military sense of both verbs against the legal one.
Gill reads the plea of Christ committing his cause to the righteous Judge; Calvin analyses the court that produced the persecution and draws a rule of consolation under calumny.
Clarke keeps the forensic sense of the first verb, collects the ancient titles, and insists the armed figure is spoken merely after the manner of men.
Henry states the situation that forced the appeal, and Spurgeon lets the legal and the martial senses alternate.
Augustine allegorises the armour, taking the shield for the good-will with which God compasses his own.

debates.question: Is the opening plea legal or martial?

positions.summary: Martial: the first verb must be rendered strive, since the construction requires it and the parallelism suggests recourse to arms rather than to law; the second is literally devour.
Legal: contend is the right word, often used in a forensic sense.
Both together, alternating — meet them in the law-court if they plead there, and oppose strength to strength if they use force.
Both, and the doubleness is the point: the enemies attacked both his life and his reputation, so he asks redress of both.

The persecution by Saul, this psalm being the lyrical expansion of what David says to Saul's face in Samuel; the conjecture of Jeremiah's authorship fails because the opening suits a persecuted king, not a prophet.
The persecution by Saul and his courtiers, though the Syriac makes it the Idumean attack and the Arabic a prophecy of the incarnation.
The conspiracy of the nobles against an innocent man, in which the common people were carried along by ignorance rather than malice.

debates.question: How literally may the armed God of the second verse be taken?

positions.summary: Only after the manner of men: God overthrows the enemies of his people by the shield and buckler of others, not any of his own.
Not that he needs them to defend himself, but that he would be shield and buckler to David, as he is to all his people.

A bold flight of imagination, nowhere in Hebrew poetry realised so vividly except in one passage of Isaiah — vivid enough that the poet overlooks the anomaly of arming a warrior with two shields at once.
Vivid metaphor: the Lord coming forth armed and interposing between his servant and his enemies, the two weapons perhaps the greater and lesser protections of providence.

outliers.summary: Notices that the poet, in the intensity of his purpose, arms the divine warrior with two shields at once — an anomaly no other reader remarks.

themes: Plead my cause, O Lord, with them that strive with me: fight against them that fight against me.
Take hold of shield and buckler, and stand up for mine help.

3.pericope_label: Draw out also the spear, and stop the way against them that persecute me... False witnesses did rise up; they laid to my charge things that I knew not

schools.summary: Delitzsch and Ellicott both re-order the text of the seventh verse and treat the imagery — the angel, the slippery way, the storm — as figures to be identified from usage rather than doctrine.
Gill justifies the imprecations as prophecies rather than examples, and supplies the local colour of the dark valleys.
Clarke defends the imprecations by an analogy from self-defence, reads the whole series as military language, and proposes the same textual re-ordering; Wesley glosses the assurance sought.
Henry reconstructs the legal proceeding behind the false witnesses; Spurgeon presses David's ignorance of the charge.

debates.question: Are the imprecations of this psalm defensible?

positions.summary: They are prophecies of what would be and expressions of faith, not examples for private persons, and so not contrary to the rule of loving enemies.
They are legitimate, being aimed not at the souls of the men but at their schemes: as one may break an assailant's arm to prevent both his own death and his enemy's murder, so David prays.

debates.question: What is the angel of the Lord who chases and persecutes?

positions.summary: A personification of the hurricane itself, which drives all obstacles before it and overwhelms whole armies in dangerous places.
Undecided — a spirit, good or bad, or anything God uses.

debates.question: Is the text of the seventh verse in order?

positions.summary: No: the word for pit belongs to the second clause, giving 'without cause they hid their net for me, without cause digged a pit for my soul'.
Read as it stands, of a pit with a net hidden in it, as used for trapping wild beasts.

outliers.summary: Observes that the bones, which elsewhere in the psalms share only the anguish of the soul, are here made to share its joy, so that gladness throbs through every member.
Finds the eighth verse so confused that the variations of the ancient versions point to a corrupt text, and would supply a whole clause from the Syriac to complete the parallelism.

themes: Draw out also the spear, and stop the way against them that persecute me: say unto my soul, I am thy salvation.
Let them be confounded and put to shame that seek after my soul: let them be turned back and brought to confusion that devise my hurt.
Let them be as chaff before the wind: and let the angel of the Lord chase them.
Let their way be dark and slippery: and let the angel of the Lord persecute them.
For without cause have they hid for me their net in a pit, which without cause they have digged for my soul.
Let destruction come upon him at unawares; and let his net that he hath hid catch himself: into that very destruction let him fall.
And my soul shall be joyful in the Lord: it shall rejoice in his salvation.
All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like unto thee, which deliverest the poor from him that is too strong for him, yea, the poor and the needy from him that spoileth him?
False witnesses did rise up; they laid to my charge things that I knew not.

12.pericope_label: They rewarded me evil for good, to the spoiling of my soul... Lord, how long wilt thou look on? rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions

schools.summary: Ellicott works through the disputed words one by one — desolation, squalid, the abjects, the barbarisms — rejecting the received renderings where the versions support better ones.
Gill particularises the ingratitude from David's history and finds the cake-mockers independently.
Clarke corrects 'soul' to 'life', explains the returning prayer by the Eastern bosom, and reads the mockery as prophetic of Christ; Wesley keeps to short glosses.
Henry gathers the whole indictment into five heads and draws from it the character of the quiet in the land.

debates.question: What does 'my prayer returned into mine own bosom' mean?

positions.summary: That the prayers were not wasted: like alms given for God's sake, they are returned tenfold into the bosom where the Asiatics carry what is given them.

Literally, that the prayer turned upon his bosom — the posture of the next verse, the words muttered into his breast; a reading he reports and calls prosaic, after rejecting fruitless prayer, self-directed answer, and silent prayer.
That his fastings and prayers did them no good.

debates.question: Who are the 'abjects' that gathered together?

positions.summary: Smiters, probably hired assassins lying in wait.
The word occurs only here; the versions all give an active sense — whips, smiters, the wicked who smite with words — and the passive rendering behind 'abjects' comes from a mediaeval rabbi.

debates.question: What are the 'hypocritical mockers in feasts'?

positions.summary: Better 'in the manner of profane barbaric barbarisms', the versions taking the word not for feasts but for barbarisms and 'hypocritical' properly meaning profane.
Cake-mockers — parasites who hang about the tables of the rich and earn their dinner by buffoonery; either they mocked David as wanting bread or mocked him for the sake of a meal.
Buffoons and jesters who derided David to gain admittance to the tables of great men.
Prophetic of Christ, blindfolded and buffeted so that he could not discern who struck him, and mocked in Herod's purple robe.

outliers.summary: Makes the psalm's enemies a study in what the godly suffer: the quiet in the land live in dutiful subjection and study peace, yet all the arts of malice are used to make them odious, their words misconstrued and laws made to ensnare them.

themes: They rewarded me evil for good to the spoiling of my soul.
But as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth: I humbled my soul with fasting; and my prayer returned into mine own bosom.
I behaved myself as though he had been my friend or brother: I bowed down heavily, as one that mourneth for his mother.
But in mine adversity they rejoiced, and gathered themselves together: yea, the abjects gathered themselves together against me, and I knew it not; they did tear me, and ceased not:
With hypocritical mockers in feasts, they gnashed upon me with their teeth.
Lord, how long wilt thou look on? rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions.

18.pericope_label: I will give thee thanks in the great congregation: I will praise thee among much people... And my tongue shall speak of thy righteousness and of thy praise all the day long

schools.summary: Delitzsch marks the calmer tone of the third part, parses the gesture and the verbs of waking, and reads the closing wish as the vindication of God's own righteousness; Ellicott identifies the winking and the quiet in the land from usage.
Gill corrects the grammar of the nineteenth verse, distinguishes two senses of righteousness in the appeal, and identifies the few adherents David had.
Clarke describes the sound of the taunt, keeps the legal figure of the appeal, and turns the closing imprecation into a prophecy fulfilled at Gilboa; Wesley glosses the vow and the artifices.
Spurgeon reads the winking eye as low-bred congratulation at a victim's ruin and turns the enemies' unpeaceableness into a rule about accusers.

debates.question: Who are 'the quiet in the land'?

positions.summary: The pious Jews who wished to preserve their national life and religion against foreign influence.
David and his followers, who desired only to live peaceably while their enemies used subtle artifices rather than open violence.
Peaceable men generally, whom troublers cannot judge to be peaceable, riotous men charging others with sedition.

debates.question: How are the closing imprecations to be taken?

positions.summary: As prophecy: a declaration against Saul and his courtiers, fulfilled when they were confounded and dishonoured in the last battle with the Philistines.
As a prayer that they be confounded together, as one man, since together they had gathered against him.
As the vindication of God's righteousness, which is proved when David's is made manifest.

outliers.summary: Notices that the poet takes up the enemies' malignant boast, 'now our eye has seen it', and turns the same words back in the next verse against them: this thou hast seen, O Lord.
Reads 'wrongfully' as attached not to 'rejoice' but to 'enemies', changing the complaint from unjust triumph to unjust enmity.

themes: I will give thee thanks in the great congregation: I will praise thee among much people.
Let not them that are mine enemies wrongfully rejoice over me: neither let them wink with the eye that hate me without a cause.
For they speak not peace: but they devise deceitful matters against them that are quiet in the land.
Yea, they opened their mouth wide against me, and said, Aha, aha, our eye hath seen it.
This thou hast seen, O Lord: keep not silence: O Lord, be not far from me.
Stir up thyself, and awake to my judgment, even unto my cause, my God and my Lord.
Judge me, O Lord my God, according to thy righteousness; and let them not rejoice over me.
Let them not say in their hearts, Ah, so would we have it: let them not say, We have swallowed him up.
Let them be ashamed and brought to confusion together that rejoice at mine hurt: let them be clothed with shame and dishonour that magnify themselves against me.
Let them shout for joy, and be glad, that favour my righteous cause: yea, let them say continually, Let the Lord be magnified, which hath pleasure in the prosperity of his servant.
And my tongue shall speak of thy righteousness and of thy praise all the day long.
